deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page reduces meridian/clock observations (June series) and gives Gauss's rules for combining weights: for threads a,b the weight is 2ab/(a+b); for a,b,c it is 8abc/(ab+4ac+bc). It also contains least-squares error estimates with the factor 0.6745 for probable error. This page sets up the reduction of ring-micrometer (Kreismikrometer) observations. In these an unknown object (A,D), probably a comet or planet, is compared with up to three known stars.

Notation as written:
- Known stars have right ascensions α, α', α'' and declinations δ, δ', δ''. The object has A and D.
- τ, τ', τ'', T are the means of the entry and exit times, i.e. the times of mid-transit across the ring.
- μ, μ', μ'', M are the 'Mora', the durations from entry to exit, in time.
- The diameter of the field (ring) in time is σ = (2/15)ρ. Here ρ is the ring radius in arc-seconds, so the diameter 2ρ'' corresponds to 2ρ/15 seconds of time.

Step 1 (chord angle): for each body Gauss defines an angle by sin λ = μ cos δ / ρ, and similarly sin λ', sin λ''. For the object, sin L = M cos D / ρ.
- Modern reading (mine): μ cos δ is the chord in time reduced to a great circle. Dividing by the diameter gives chord/diameter = sin λ.
- So the half-chord is ρ sin λ and the perpendicular distance of the track from the ring centre is ρ cos λ.
- λ = 90° is a central passage; λ = 0 is a grazing one.
- With σ defined just above, the dimensionally consistent form is μ cos δ / σ (see errors).

Step 2 (the quantities being determined, mine): A − α = T − τ for right ascension. D − δ = ±ρ(cos L − cos λ) for declination, with signs according to which side of the centre each track lies.

Step 3 (weights as stated by Gauss):
- Weight of the right ascension obtained from the first star: 2 cos²λ cos²L / (cos²L + cos²λ + cos²λ' + cos²λ'').
- Weight of the declination from the first star: 2 sin²λ sin²L / (sin²L + sin²λ + sin²λ' + sin²λ'').
- Structure: each body gets an individual weight, w = cos²λ (RA) or sin²λ (Dec), normalised so the best case has weight 1.
- With only one comparison star, the formula reduces to 2 w_1 W/(w_1 + W). This is the same combination rule 2ab/(a+b) found on the previous page: half the reciprocal-sum weight of a difference, rescaled by 2.
- With several comparison stars, Gauss replaces w_1 + W in the denominator by the sum of all four individual weights. This apparently accounts for the object's (or ring-centre's) contribution being shared among the stars. It is a heuristic or approximate allocation, not derived on the page.

The page gives no derivation of the individual weights and ends there; the next page has only the folio number.
errors: Denominators: right after defining σ = (2/15)ρ as the field diameter in time, Gauss writes μ cos δ/ρ = sin λ. Dimensional consistency (μ in seconds of time, ρ the radius in arc-seconds) requires μ cos δ/σ. The smudges under the first two denominators look like corrections, possibly σ altered to ρ or vice versa. Either ρ is meant in time units or σ is intended.

The assignment of individual weights cannot be confirmed and may be swapped (my analysis, hedged). Under sin λ = chord/diameter, suppose the natural error model is a radial uncertainty ε of the apparent contact with the ring edge.
- The along-track error per contact is ε/sin λ, so the RA weight should be ∝ sin²λ and the Dec weight ∝ cos²λ.
- Under a pure timing-error model instead, the RA weight is constant and the Dec weight ∝ cot²λ.
- Gauss's cos² (RA) and sin² (Dec) match neither, unless λ is effectively the complementary angle or a different error model is intended.

The multi-star denominator (sum of all four individual weights) is not derived. It is not the exact least-squares weight of A − α when several comparison stars share one object observation; it seems to be an approximate rule.

results.what: Reduction of ring-micrometer observations: the chord angle sin λ = μ cos δ/(diameter) and the mid-transit time give the RA difference T − τ and the declination difference ρ(cos L − cos λ).
results.usually_credited_to: Boscovich (ring micrometer, 18th c.); standard reduction formulas by Olbers and Bessel, c. 1800–1830

results.what: Weights for RA and Dec from each comparison star, depending on the chord angles via cos² and sin², combined by a 2ab/(a+b)-type rule extended to several stars.
results.modern_name: Weighting of observations / propagation of error in least squares
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (theory of least squares, 1809/1823); the specific ring-micrometer weights are routine practical astronomy

deep.surprise_reason: Practical observatory reduction notes for ring-micrometer comparisons with weight formulas. This is routine work for Gauss at Göttingen in the 1810s–20s, and the weight scheme is heuristic rather than a new result.

checkable.asserts: With half-chord rho*sin(lam), the chord/diameter ratio equals sin(lam) (squared form identity; trivially zero).
The derivative of the track distance d = sqrt(rho^2 - h^2) with respect to the half-chord h is -tan(lambda), so the Dec error grows like tan(lambda) times the chord error.
With a single comparison star, Gauss's formula 2*w1*W/(W+w1) coincides with the 2ab/(a+b) rule on the previous page.
With sigma = 2*rho/15, a diameter of 2*rho arc-seconds corresponds to sigma seconds of time (factor 15 arcsec per time-second).

transcription_corrections: The denominators in sin λ, sin λ' are written as ρ over a smudged, apparently corrected symbol (possibly σ). The third and fourth clearly read ρ; the intended quantity is likely σ for dimensional consistency.
The squared terms are written as cos λ² etc. in Gauss's notation, meaning cos²λ. The second denominator term reads 'cos λ^2' with the exponent partly faint.
